Brownwood Community Garden Report for September 2026

October 4, 2026 at 6:10 pm Derrick Stuckly
  • Local News
  • Tweet
  • Share
  • Reddit
  • +1
  • Pocket
  • LinkedIn

Article by Jan Green

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:37
Instaread

It’s been a hot September, most days well above normal highs (or so it seemed while working out in the garden), and still harvests are fairly abundant. Like the Energizer Bunny, our cucumber harvest just keeps going and going. Unlike our gardeners and faithful volunteers, the Cucuzzi and luffa squash are thoroughly enjoying the sizzling summer heat. The Tahitian melon squash which was planted late is just now beginning to start production. Then, with a tinge of sadness, reality hits. Growing season will soon be coming to an end! No!!! The approaching rain and cold front which visited us the last couple days of September remind us that those colder conditions are inevitable and will, at the very least, slow production down before taking it out completely. We hope for another month of harvest time, but there’s no guarantee. Old man winter can make a quick, unexpected visit most any time- in one day and out the next. It’s at this time, while the garden is still up and running, that we start to assess the current year and consider what went well (the cucumbers for example, from the shintokiwa in spring to the Indian Snake throughout the relentless heat of the summer), and what did not do so well.

The decision to grow moschata species of squash rather than the more traditional yellow and zucchini in the pepo family worked well for us, mostly. The Tromboncino was hit early in the season by vine borers and did not survive. Other than that, the luffa, cucuzzi, Seminole pumpkin squash, and Tahitian melon squash have done exceptionally well resisting vine borers and squash bugs. For the first time In years, we have been able to supply Good Samaritan and Salvation Army with squash. They look different than what most people are accustomed to which caused a bit of a problem. People tend to take a look at them and walk right on by, not realizing they can be used like zucchini in their cooking – definitely something we need to work on next year.

A popular crop, the cantaloupe, is something we’d like to grow more of next year. That sweet, juicy treat is in demand. We just have to do a better job managing the critters, from the bugs to the possums (we think) that keep helping themselves to our produce just days before we’re ready to harvest.

Peppers have been abundant this year but a tad small as the Texas heat kicked in. Shade cloth would be helpful, just not too practical for us. As October arrives with its cooler temperatures, we’re looking for a change there. Actually, we’ve already noticed the bells and jalapeños growing larger recently. We don’t want those temperatures to cool off too much though. That could put the peppers into shock and slow down production. It’s a bit of a balancing act. We can’t have it too hot or too cold, something we have no control over. Advertisements

Let’s not even talk about those tomatoes that don’t seem to be cooperating as of yet. We now see and have been seeing blossoms for a while, yet very few tomatoes to show for it. My guess is, up to now, the weather has still been a bit too hot, causing a pollination problem for the tomatoes. As temperatures gradually begin cooling down, we then become concerned of an early frost or temperatures cooling off too quickly which would bring that hope for a fall tomato harvest to an end. For now we harvest just a few each day, not enough to fulfill the demand. Early problems with leaf footed bugs and then the high temperatures resulted in a less than abundant harvest this year, so much to our dismay, fewer BLTs and less salsa were enjoyed around town.

Recently, the okra production has been slowing down. The tops of many of the plants have been pruned, and new growth is showing up. We’re hoping those harvests pick up a bit. They say, “It’s not over until the fat lady sings”. Well, we’ve seen her in the vicinity, but we don’t hear her warming up quite yet, so we still hope there’s time for okra production to pick up before cold temperatures take it down for the season.

The first round of figs was damaged by the frost, but the second crop is currently doing well, and those that like figs are enjoying one of the few fruits we’ve been able to grow successfully this year in our orchard.

Not a lot of changes are on the horizon for next year. Hopefully we can grow a little more fruit and, as always, we hope to control the most damaging pests that come our way. For years that was the cucumber beetle followed by vine borers and squash bugs. This year it’s the leaf footed bugs. We’ll study about controlling them, and when it seems we’ve about won that war, another bug will likely crawl into our garden and our lives. At times it seems endless.

All in all, it’s been a good year so far, over 1000 pounds this month and over 7000 pounds this year. We’re counting on supplying even more fresh produce to this community in the upcoming month or so. Squash, peppers, tomatoes, melons, cucumbers (of course) are all needing more of that warm weather that we wished for months would go away. Isn’t it interesting that now we’re hoping and praying for just a few more of those warm days we previously were wishing away?
